utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Mr. Tieger, you have a new team member.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not new, Mr. President, but you correctly noted here today I'm joined by Ms. Kimberly West.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. How are you, sir? Did you have a good weekend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, good afternoon, Your Honour. I got some very good rest. I certainly did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Harvey. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I can try again with this microphone. Good afternoon, Your Honours. May I introduce Mrs. Sofie Breslau who has been with my team for many months. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Excellencies. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems that we don't have much time today, so I will have to move on to a few key matters straight away. Is it correct, have you noticed, that people who looked for their acquaintances -- actually, people who looked for someone by their names and their surnames, were they looking for their enemies or their acquaintances or their friends?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I have no idea whether they were enemies or friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have to move on to the main event that you described. You were at that school and then they drove you on the small TAM truck; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one thing. You feel free to remind me too. Let's just wait for the interpretation and the transcript to finish. So when you see the letter A, you can start giving your answer. How far away is that meadow where they were carrying out these executions, how far away from the school?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly, but gun-shots could be heard at the gym where we were sitting, and they said, "Look, they killed all of those people who were taken out ."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in which TAM truck were you in?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of that, I don't know. It was perhaps two hours before dark that my turn came, but I don't know in what order the TAM trucks were taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were 296 of you there, right, or more than that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 296 of us were brought in from Bratunac, and then people were brought on trucks, buses, whatever, I don't know. Started at daybreak until about 10.00 until the gym was full. Once the gym was full, they no longer brought any people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, then, you were being blindfolded in the gym itself?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as we were walking out of the gym, they put blindfolds on our faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. They did not tie your hands?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In one of your statements you said that there were different blindfolds, but what were they usually made of?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thin cloth, that's what it was, in different colours. The width was about 10 centimetres and the length was sufficient to be able to tie it around the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then did they take off those blindfolds there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. When you arrived, you saw that two pits had been dug; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two excavators that were digging two holes there at two different places. Now, whether they had been dug that night or not, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to a certain point you came on this TAM truck and from there onwards you walked?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I came on the TAM truck to the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say at some point that the TAM truck could not go any further but that you had to walk a bit?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And when you arrived and you were not on the first TAM truck, what did you see? Where were these people who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of me, there was this field there, a lot of pastures, actually, and they were killed as they stood in lines, and that's where they got us off the truck and then they shot people in the back. And when everybody fell, then individually they went around to see who was still moving and then they would kill such persons. They would go on shooting for as long as anybody was moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And they did not take off anybody's blindfolds, all the blindfolds were still on these people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't take anybody's blindfold off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that blindfold should be found during the exhumation; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless it rotted away, that would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that General Mladic was following these TAM trucks in a red car; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These TAM trucks were followed -- were followed by a soldier all the way up until they were unloaded, and it was in this red car. And the red car would return before the TAM would go to follow another TAM that was being taken to another place. When they unloaded me there and when they carried out those executions, a few other TAM trucks came. And then General Mladic came with this same red car. He sat in the back seat and he walked out with this soldier who was sitting next to the driver. They were watching the unloading, the killing. The TAM truck left and the red car and Mladic waited until everybody was killed, all the people who were brought in on the TAM trucks. And then they got into the car and went back the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that was on the 14th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that Mladic was with Carl Bildt and President Milosevic at Dobanovci on that day attending a meeting?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time was he there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, he was there almost all day, he was there almost all day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we have the basis for that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basis is the report from Mr. Bildt's book and other reports, Akashi 's report. This is a well-known meeting that was held on the 14th of July and on the 15th of July. They had meetings then as well, but the 14th of July was most certainly the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps they met during the night. During the day he was by the school, by that gym, Mladic was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you hold a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did you leave Bratunac? When did you go to that school, on the 13th in the evening; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 65 ter 22396 and could it not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did you first see General Mladic on that day at the meadow there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in the gym. I watched him from the gym as he came to the door and we were all shouting, all of us together, "Why are you making us suffer here? Why don't you get us out of here?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the gym in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in Orahovo, the place where we were there. And then he said: "Had it been possible to reach an agreement, you wouldn't have been here. Some of you are going to Kladusa to Fikret Abdic and others will go to Bijeljina. Your transportation will arrive now and they'll take you there."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in which village were you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean where that hall was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the name was Orahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of this statement, you said that it was the village of Krizevici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near Krizevici.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see here, it's line 15 from the bottom, it says "Krizevici"? And you say -- actually, how many people were standing in the TAM truck?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't count, but perhaps it was 25 to 30. It couldn't have been more than that, and we were sitting, we were not standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. And you say that they took people, 25, 30 of them, and you say that there were how many of you there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we weren't counting. No one could do any counting in there, but everybody's estimate was about 2500, over 2.000, up to 2500.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did they start taking people away?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly when that started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did Mladic appear in that hall?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that now either. If I said something in particular, then that's the way it was; if not, I really cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did they stop taking people away? When did it stop?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the night. I'm not sure about that either, but say between 11.00 and 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And all of it was over; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what they said. When the last TAM truck came, then the driver from the TAM truck said, "There's no one left. Everybody has been brought in and killed." And then they asked him, "Are we going to come with you?" And he said, "No, not with me." And then they said, "What are we going to do here, wait?" And he said, "I don't know. Nobody told me to drive you." The TAM truck left and then they stood there by the excavators and waited while the other TAM truck showed up. Later they turned off the lights on the excavator. They got onto the TAM truck and they all left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where were you all that time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When night fell, I crawled out from beneath the dead and I went behind some bushes and hid there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what you said here on this page. You say that on the 14th of July in the afternoon hours Mladic came again and said from the door, "Some of you are going to Fikret Abdic and some of you will be going to Bijeljina," so it was the afternoon; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you what time. I've described it. I have already described it. I described this before, when it was, roughly. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. And in your opinion how many tours were there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how long did it take for a whole round to be completed, for the people to be killed, and for the truck to go back?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't be enough time for you to smoke a cigarette before the second tour arrived, but I didn't look on my watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you said that there were between 100 and 120 such tours?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if there were 20 or 30 people in each truck and it all started after Mladic's arrival and ended at around 11.00, can you now see how this arithmetic of yours works? What is wrong with it, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two trucks drove people away. Now, you do the counting. I am not a mathematician.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this statement be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we shall put it under seal for the moment. I think we -- Defence can produce a public, redacted version easily. We'll admit both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The under seal version will be Exhibit D1944 and the public redacted version will be Exhibit D1945.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly move to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, on various occasions you were shown various photographs. I'm interested to hear what did you learn in Tuzla before the first interview. Who was it who told you about the gym, about the hedge, what kind of information was given to you in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But somebody must have gave you this description.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I described how the gym looked like and then the people who used to play basketball in that gym during peace time confirmed that that was the same gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But concerning the meadow and the hedge and the fly-over, you inquired about that and somebody else described these issues to you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they asked me where the shooting was and I said that all I could see was a fly-over and the people would say, "Oh, well, we know exactly the place. This is the railway that leads to Zvornik and it must have been close to the railway."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see Mladic only once on that meadow?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in one of your statements you said that you had seen him five times?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. I want some references. It's an extremely misleading way of putting questions to say: You said you saw him on the meadow once and in the statement you said you saw him five times, trying to imply to the witness that he said: I saw him five times at the meadow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- sorry, I overlapped. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is his second statement given on the 25 June [as interpreted] 1995. ERN number is 017222 to 7225, lines 6 and 7 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the page number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said four or five times: I saw Ratko Mladic coming in a red car behind the truck and he was watching the shooting with no hat on his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you upload it. Do you have a 65 ter number for that, Mr. Nicholls or Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll find it right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, it's 22398 and it's page 3 of the English that Mr. Karadzic is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a statement given in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the 25th of July. Can we have page 3. It's page 3 in English, definitely, but in Serbian, it might be page 2:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "I saw Ratko Mladic, bare-headed, come up behind the tamic four or five times in a red car and watch the executions." [Interpretation] You say that Ratko Mladic spent the entire afternoon and the evening of the 14th of July watching the executions about which he actually said that you would go to either Fikret Abdic or to Bijeljina, but now you say that he was watching it.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was interpreted, but in total I can say that I saw him for six times, not five times, from Potocari to Orahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you mean interpreted? You gave your statement in Serbian, in our own language.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how it was noted down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anybody change your statements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page in the Serbian for the benefit of the witness, and I kindly ask for this not to be broadcast. No, the previous one. Maybe number 2 in Serbian. We have found the exact portion in English and now we're going to find the corresponding one in Serbian. It's on page 3. Page 3, please, tenth line from the bottom -- eighth line from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is what you said in our language. "As I was lying there, I saw Mladic coming in a red car, bare-headed, four or five times, and watched the execution. I saw the five Chetniks who had been carrying out the executions leave in the tamic and then I shouted, 'Is anybody alive?' A young man responded." So you were lying underneath the dead bodies for the whole time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until darkness fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And only then did you come out and went in hiding behind the bush. There was no one there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were still killing people but there were no lights on. I was in the darkness. I was not in the spotlight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this is what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they brought people four or five times, after which time Mladic arrived in a red car. I didn't say that Mladic came four or five times, but after four or five trips by the truck people asked me how many TAM trucks had been driven before Mladic arrived and I said four or five TAM trucks had arrived. And then Mladic arrived with the next TAM truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many dead bodies were on top of you? How did you manage to hide and you escaped being noticed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they moved away, I see that they were lining people one next to another in four rows. So as they were falling down, they were falling on top of each other. The first one then the second one and the third one, and so on, the fourth one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many dead bodies hide you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was hidden by one body and he was hidden by another body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that there were at least two or three layers of bodies on top of you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three layers, and I was the closest one to the dead people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this statement be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll do the same exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The under seal statement will be Exhibit D1946 and the public redacted version will be D1947.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, according to your knowledge, not about -- not according to your opinion, how many people were killed on that meadow?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never learned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did they dig those holes up?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to put the dead people into those holes, to bury them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they didn't do it in front of you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the dead people were left on the meadows, the holes had been dug up, but they nevertheless went away in a TAM truck; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know if those people were buried there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably they did because they had dug up those holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you described this murder, I examined the transcript and you said that you saw the man who had been killed with an iron bar being taken out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they took him out behind the warehouse in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So they went behind the warehouse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately to the left as you go through the doorway. They didn't go behind the warehouse. They went to the left and I was coming back from the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now a minute ago in line 10 you said "behind the warehouse." Now, tell me, you remained in the warehouse, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how then did you find out about his killing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that had been hit with an iron bar and an axe, you mean that one? Well, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you were inside the warehouse and they were behind the warehouse; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you walk into the warehouse, this corridor went all the way to a small room. As we were walking to the right from the warehouse to the room, they would take people only to the left, not behind the warehouse. They remained there. It was only to the left of the warehouse. It was just off the corridor. They didn't go behind the warehouse and that's why I was able to see it. They put a hand on their shoulder, and I think that two or three men were standing on both sides. One of them had an automatic rifle and he was turned to the man who was approaching him and he was shouting, "Come closer, come closer." He started towards the soldier, and from the left one of them hit him with an iron bar on the back and he fell down. The other one on the right had an axe and hit him on the spine. He left the axe there. He couldn't or wouldn't take the blade out. After that I went into the warehouse and this is how this incident ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see the rails from the meadow or not?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just saw the fly-over and the iron fence next to it. I only know that we passed underneath in the TAM truck, but I didn't know what was there above. Later when I asked people, others told me that there was a fly-over and the rails go over it and you passed underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In one statement, and that's 65 ter 22396, page 2, paragraph 2, you said you had been brought there -- you had been taken away at what time?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you what time it was now. I remembered it then and I said it then and that's correct.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. Must have been earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this statement you said around 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now in which statement I said what, whether everything was recorded properly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If it was July and if it was earlier, it was still daylight or was it already dark?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got to that meadow, the sun was still shining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement 1D4875 you said it was already dark and the only light were the headlights on the bulldozer.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was getting dark. The bulldozer came, turned on its headlights, and the light was reflected, but they didn't use the headlights while it was still light.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at this statement 1D4875, and we'll see that on page 4, paragraph 7: [In English] "The only light was from the bulldozer. After the shooting, if the Serbs heard voices of people who were still alive, they looked for them and shoot them ...," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "At 7.30 p.m., we left the gym and were blindfolded as we left from the left door of the gym. I removed my blindfolds immediately (apparently he pushed them up a little) so I could see what was going on. The Serbs were busy hurrying us up. They said 'hurry, hurry.' We got into trucks and I saw the little red car following behind. At every turning I saw dead bodies on the road. Then the Serbs opened the back side ..." [Interpretation] So you saw dead bodies even as you were travelling there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one juncture I saw as many dead bodies as on the site where I was taken. Not all the way along the road. At one point, in one place, which was a grazing ground, there were as many bodies as I saw later. The TAM truck continued until it came to the second heap of dead bodies, then we were unloaded, the truck turned around, and we were all killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And nobody tried to run?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all exhausted. Nobody could run and there were people all around waiting with automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said it took only five to ten minutes there and it was already dark, and the only light was from the bulldozer?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it was dark when I arrived. I said they turned on the headlights for the killing only when it got dark.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this statement be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit both versions, in public and under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The under seal version will be Exhibit D1948 and the public redacted version will be Exhibit D1949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who was this interview given to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see the last page, please, [In English] "David Rohde, the Christian Science Monitor, the Pulitzer Prize Winner ...," and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have many more questions, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll make it short. Just a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you were hesitating to testify, it was because your expenses were not paid; correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Earlier in the report dated 11 October 1998, ERN 0067-6051, it's only one page, it says you were reluctant to testify because your expenses were not paid.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hearing this for the first time from you. I wouldn't be coming here if something like that had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no objection. Just maybe Mr. Karadzic could read out exactly what's said in the information report. It's not a statement, it's an info report, so the witness knows. He's paraphrased a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no reason to doubt that the Prosecution recorded exactly what the witness said. It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, if you are not going to pursue that matter further, we can continue leaving it at that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call the document. I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- like to tender this 65 ter 22400 without broadcasting. Not be broadcast. It says: "The witness expressed reluctance to come to The Hague to testify because of the problems last time related to the reimbursement of expenses."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say it the way they recorded it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you need to be fair, you have to read out the remaining paragraphs and put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, I can read it out. He claimed that he heard heavy machinery working when he was at the school, but that doesn't matter. I'm interested in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have now followed. Yes, we can admit this --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1950 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we can -- yes, that's then -- may be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were in the hangar when they took away this man. How far were they from you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Bratunac; is that what you're asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you saw one murder.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far away from you were they?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than 5 or 6 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. However, in your statement dated 22nd July, 1995 - and that's your first statement, right? - you said they were 2 metres away?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two metres from the door leading to the left. That's what I may have said, not that it was 2 metres between me and them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's now for you to come to your last questions. Conclude in two minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm a bit nonplussed, Witness, because you say about the statements you have given, if that's what is written then you reckon it is correct. Is everything you've ever said correct, accurate?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I quoted any figures, that's accurate. Whenever I made assumptions about something, it could be more but not less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about things other than figures?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on what you mean. If I assumed something was true, that's certainly true. If I made assumptions about quantities or estimated quantities, I cannot guarantee for the accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just very quickly, sir. Could I have P01488 up on the screen. That's one of General Mladic's notebooks. Witness, at page 5 today it was put to you that Mladic was with Carl Bildt and President Milosevic at Dobanovci on the 14th of July and you asked: "Well, what time was he there?" And Mr. Karadzic said: "Well, he was there almost all day, almost all day." And a few lines later on you said: "Perhaps they met during the night. During the day he was by the school, by the gym."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have the English page 2, please. And if we can just actually scroll so we can see the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is from the 14 July 1995 meeting with President Milosevic, Bildt, and General de Lapresle. So you haven't seen this before, sir, but it is a notebook, a diary kept by General Mladic. If you could see it on the right, just below where it says 14 July 1995, could you read out what time the meeting was. If it's too small, let me know. Well, I'll read it out for you. It says 21.15 hours, so after 9.00 p.m. and my question is, Witness: After you'd been lined up in a line with other men and they had shot at you and you had fallen under a pile of bodies and you were lying there and the trucks were coming and leaving, were you checking your watch? Were you trying to keep track of every second and how many times the trucks were coming?

utterances.speaker: KDZ039 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I saw that when they had killed one batch they would light a cigarette, and before they were done with one cigarette a new TAM truck would come and they would throw the unfinished cigarette on to the ground. That's how much time it took.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask one additional question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. You asked --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About timing. It's a new thing that arises from redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you raised this question and -- I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. The Chamber will not allow you to put further questions. Well, Mr. Witness, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague yet again to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have about 20 minutes before the break. Shall we continue or do you suggest having a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ms. West will call the next witness. She indicates it's fine to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The next witness will be Colonel Johannes Rutten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you kindly make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I state that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. If you could make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, may we have 65 ter 90296, please. Mr. President, I understand the Srebrenica trial video booklet has been distributed to the Bench and to the Defence. That is a compilation of all the Srebrenica-relevant videos. I'll be using one of them today. I will give the time-codes, but it's not our intention to admit each video separately. We'll just authenticate each video with the witnesses and then it's our intention at the end of the case to admit all the videos as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What is your name and your current rank.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: My name is Rutten and my current rank is lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, you have testified in the Krstic case, the Popovic case, and the Tolimir case; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And an amalgamated statement was prepared containing the relevant portions of your prior testimonies, and this statement you reviewed and signed on the 8th of November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is this the statement on the screen in front of you the one you reviewed and signed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, that's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this statement accurately reflects an amalgamation of the testimonies that you've previously given?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you were asked today about the same matters contained in the statement, would you provide the same information to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I would provide the same information to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender the statement and the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter 90296 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3948, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And as for -- can I hear from the Defence as to the admission of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't have any objection to any of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you have no objection to the -- to adding these to the 65 ter list of 23512?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we don't, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's granted. In relation to 65 ter number 3233, 3233, which is being dealt with in the para 4.13, I'm not sure how it forms indispensable, inseparable with his statement. It's para 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this part of his statement he was asked -- excuse me, in this part of his testimony he was asked in comparison between the ABiH and the VRS and he was talking about, particularly here, whether he had ever seen BiH soldiers with UN equipment. And he indicated that he had not. I would submit that that's an indispensable part of the statement that he's given in the past because it shows that there had been no occasion in which he believed that he, himself, had ever seen BiH posing as UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you deal with it directly in -- if you are to tender this document - with the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. Should I read a summary of the statement first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Johannes Rutten joined the Royal Dutch Army in 1979 as a conscript and served as a non-commissioned officer in a variety of posts before entering officers' training school in 1991. He completed his studies two years later and was commissioned as a 2nd lieutenant. From January through July 1995, the Colonel served with DutchBat III in Potocari as a 1st lieutenant, during which time he was a commander of an anti-tank platoon, patrol co-ordinator, and intelligence officer. During the spring of 1995, the food situation in Srebrenica became increasingly dire because the Bosnian Serbs did not allow humanitarian aid convoys permission to enter the enclave. These difficulties forced desperate Muslim civilians to rummage through the DutchBat garbage dump in search of anything edible. Colonel Rutten took photos of what he described as an unbelievable event. According to the colonel, the Muslims in Srebrenica had no real army structure, possessed only small armaments, and almost no ammunition. In contrast, the VRS was well structured and well equipped. By the end of June 1995, there was a build-up of VRS forces, including more tanks and more artillery on the hills around the enclave. On July 10th, the Colonel heard severe impacts behind the Potocari compound from a rocket-launcher based in Bratunac. Following the shelling, DutchBat found an unexploded rocket just behind the compound. The shelling became heavier on the following day and stopped during the late evening. The shelling did not target military objectives, but instead seemed intended to keep DutchBat soldiers from patrolling outside of the compound. As a result, the Dutch soldiers would not be able to witness VRS actions. In the evening, the Colonel heard that the situation in Srebrenica was getting out of hand and that refugees were on the move towards Potocari. He then received an order to cut a hole in the rear side of the compound fence to let the refugees in, if necessary. The first refugees began to arrive but remained at the bus remise just outside the southern border of the UN compound. By the end of the evening, the Colonel closed the compound fence again. On the following day, July 11th, large refugee groups began making their way to Potocari from Srebrenica. DutchBat sent trucks from the compound to Srebrenica. The trucks returned full of refugees. The Colonel opened the hole in the compound fence again and refugees entered the UN compound. By the end of the day, 4- to 5.000 refugees were inside the compound and plenty more outside of it in the area of the bus remise. Three groups of ten DutchBat soldiers each, one group which was led by the witness, secured the perimeter of the refugees outside the compound with red and white tape, which was the only means available to make it clear that the area was meant to be secure under UN surveillance. On the morning of July 12th, the Colonel heard small arms fired, followed by mortar fire. There were houses burning around the bus remise and in other places as well. This, coupled with the arrival of Bosnian Serb "Rambo-type" soldiers, led to a feeling of panic among the refugees. More VRS soldiers arrived at the compound. General Mladic also came with a film crew. The distribution of bread, water, and candy from the Bosnian Serb soldiers to the refugees was filmed. Immediately after the filming stopped, the handing out of the bread, water, and candy also stopped. At one point in the day, the Colonel and his men were detained by the Bosnian Serbs for a few hours after the Bosnian Serbs had stolen the Dutch soldiers' equipment. The Colonel had refused to give up his equipment and a gun was put to his head by a Bosnian Serb soldier as encouragement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for reading a little slower.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The buses arrived on the 12th and stopped in the early evening. Almost all men, with the exception of the very elderly, were separated from the other refugees and were sent to what became known as the "White House." On the morning of the 13th, two buses loaded with men left the "White House" and was followed by a DutchBat escort. When the escort was hijacked by the Bosnian Serbs, the Colonel decided to go to the "White House" himself to see what was taking place there. At the gate at the entrance to the "White House," he saw a huge pile of rucksacks and belongings. A few metres further were all kinds of identity cards and passports on the ground. Although he was initially refused entry, the Colonel eventually was able to get inside the "White House." He saw a Muslim man hanging from the staircase by one arm and the Colonel asked a Serb soldier to lower the man to the ground. The Colonel tried to enter a room from which he had heard voices, but another Bosnian Serb used his gun to prevent the Colonel from doing so. At one point, the Colonel managed to get upstairs, where he found two rooms filled with 50 men and boys from ages 55 to 12. He photographed the group but stopped because a Bosnian Serb soldier arrived with more men. The witness then left the house. Later that evening, the Bosnian Serbs set fire to the belongings and IDs which were outside the "White House." The fire burned for two days. The Colonel was later informed by a local interpreter of rumours that Muslim men had been killed in the vicinity of a well somewhere nearby. The Colonel and two other DutchBat soldiers went to the area and saw nine male bodies in civilian clothing lying on the ground with their faces towards a stream. All had small-calibre gun-shots to their backs or sides. The men were approximately 45 to 50 years old. The Colonel touched the bodies, which were still warm. Blood was still running from the corpses and they were no flies. In his view, the men had been shot recently and there was no evidence that the bodies had been moved to that location. The Colonel took a photo of the bodies while another soldier collected the identification cards that were scattered on the ground nearby. The Colonel and the soldiers were forced to abandon the identification cards and flee the area after shots were fired in their direction. The Colonel reported what he had seen to his higher-ups. When the Colonel ultimately returned to the Netherlands, he turned the film roll over to the Dutch army intelligence branch for developing. He was later informed that an error had occurred during the development process and that the photos were mis-developed. After photographing the bodies, the Colonel went to the area where the refugees were being ushered to the buses. There he took pictures of the Bosnian Serb soldiers' interactions with the refugees along the line of buses. The Colonel saw the Bosnian Serb soldiers separate men from their families. The Colonel also observed what he believed to be a DutchBat lieutenant and some DutchBat soldiers assisting in the deportation of the population by helping the Muslim refugees leave the area. This resulted in a confrontation between the Colonel and the lieutenant, but the process continued. Before attempting to escort the last bus leaving the compound, the Colonel went back to the "White House." By that time, the pile of belongings out front was even bigger than before and many more IDs and passports were scattered on the ground. The Colonel and another DutchBat soldier went to the previously empty left side of the house and saw that the staircase was filled completely with Muslim men. The Colonel could see the total fear on the faces of the Muslim men. The Colonel then walked to the front of the house and saw that the balcony completely filled with men and boys. He estimated that almost 300 men were in the house and on its balcony. He attempted to escort the last bus containing male refugees, but was stopped by Bosnian Serb soldiers threatening him at gunpoint. He then accompanied a truck and some medical personnel who were going into Srebrenica to pick up the last elderly people left behind. Again, he was accosted by Bosnian Serb soldiers. They took his car and he was forced to continue to Srebrenica in the truck he was meant to accompany. In Srebrenica, the Colonel saw Bosnian Serbs looting the compound and driving a Dutch APC filled with stolen material. The Bosnian Serbs had also emptied the weapons collection point where DutchBat had stored weapons it had confiscated from the Muslims in an effort to keep the enclave demilitarised. Your Honour, that concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, was my statement an accurate summary of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this has been ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Are you hearing anything at all, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, it was a correct translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Dutch interpretation took a bit more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, may I ask you this: Would you prefer to do this in English or in Dutch?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I get a little bit confused by hearing Dutch and reading English. I would rather speak in English then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's up to you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's no problem to me, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So would you like to change the channel into English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be ... [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I will ask you again. Was my statement an accurate summary of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was an accurate summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, what is your current position in the military?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: My current position is lieutenant-colonel, and I am head of personnel affairs in the Dutch army.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Where are you posted?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I am now posted in Muenster, Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, I am now going to show you a short video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is part of 65 ter 40582, the compilation of Srebrenica videos, and it's clip -- it's the clip at 20 minutes and 39 seconds and it will go to 24 minutes and 48 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I misspoke. The codes are 20 minutes and 39 seconds to 24 minutes exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, is this footage consistent with your memory?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is consistent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the red and white tape that we saw around the people, is that the tape that DutchBat put up?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is the tape we used.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was the purpose of the tape?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The purpose was to mark what was guarded by DutchBat personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did the image of the handing out of bread and candy create an accurate impression of the way the Bosnian Serb soldiers were treating the refugees at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It looks here on the video if this was the standard procedure, but you see a total different view on the ground at the moment that I was there. It was only a short instant that it -- that this happened and shortly afterwards, after the cameraman stopped filming, the bread and the handing out of the candy stopped immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what was your impression as to the purpose of the filming of those moments?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: With my knowledge of the day --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What -- I don't see any leading question. What is your objection, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection is that what is being sought is an impression, whereas we are seeking facts here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She's asking his opinion of what he saw. So I take -- I took the question to be asking that. Let's continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Colonel Rutten, would you like the question to be interpreted in Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, it's perfectly in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand it perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we don't need the English translation -- Dutch translation. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, I'll ask the question again. What was your impression as to the purpose of the filming of those moments?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I started my answer, with the knowledge of today, I would say that was perfect info operation, but with the knowledge from them, I saw it as a purely propaganda moment because as I earlier stated it stopped immediately after the filming had stopped as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, at the time, did you have access to Dutch news at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, we had no access in that time I was outside, but a few days later we had satellite communication on the compound, and we saw Dutch TV where we saw these special filming, what we just saw here on the tape, on the TV and we were wondering that that was that fast, that we saw what happened on the ground on the Dutch television.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at the time, were there any refugees left at the compound?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: At that time there were no refugees left anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, would this be a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we passed the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for 25 minutes. Thank you for your reminder, Ms. West. We'll resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where were we? Let us continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel, you talked about your impression, but that's the one you formed at the time, not the one you make now with hindsight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's the -- the word "impression," it looks a little bit strange now, but it was the situation on the ground as I described in my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, in paragraphs 46 and 47 of the statement, you speak about being detained by VRS soldiers on the 12th of July at the Potocari compound and you talk about having your headsets and your weapons taken from you and then you and your men were detained for a few hours. Were there other occasions where DutchBat soldiers had material, including uniforms and hats, stolen from them by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There were other occasions that were reported to the company and to the battalion, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And why were you concerned when uniforms were taken?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: My concern was that when uniforms are taken or our equipment, VRS soldiers could then disguise themselves to UN personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And why was it important that they not be able to disguise themselves?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We were, at that point, very few of DutchBat personnel, so our position was that we were impartial to the -- to the refugees and to the population of Srebrenica. And by having our uniforms or our equipment, it could be the case then that VRS personnel would then be as seen as DutchBat personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to -- we're going to show you 65 ter 03233 and you mentioned this in paragraph 12 of the statement, and this was a report that you had been asked about in one of your earlier testimonies. And in paragraph 4.13 of this report, this is a debriefing of the Srebrenica -- of Srebrenica by the Dutch military. In paragraph 4.13 it says: [As read] "BiH soldiers, complete with blue caps or blue hats, came within a distance of 15 metres from one of the observation points. Resembling UN personnel, they opened fire from this position in the direction of the BSA front line, so that it seemed as if the UN had opened fire. In this way, they attempted to draw fire from the BSA on the OP and thus involve DutchBat in the combat actions." Colonel, when you were asked about that in the Krstic case, you said: "I was not aware of this kind of incident." I'll ask you now, is this the type of incident that you would be concerned about when anyone stole your uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It could be the type of incident, but this particular situation, what described, here is not known to me specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were you aware of any other incidents where BiH soldiers tried to impersonate UN soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That -- yeah, that will be admitted as one of the associated exhibits, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, in the days after the event, you were interviewed several times. And first you were interviewed in Zagreb. Do you remember while in Zagreb filling out an ICTY UN questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And one of the questions in that questionnaire regarded the identity of the soldiers who detained you, the incident we were just talking about. Did you have a conversation with those soldiers, those VRS soldiers, about their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. We had a conversation because I tried to speak with more VRS personnel or what seemed to be VRS personnel. Later on it was -- it seemed to me that they were police units because -- and they spoke that they were from Belgrade and they were not normal VRS soldiers or military.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did they use a particular word to describe themselves?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, they said that they were belonging to a special unit. They call that "specijalna." And we describe that normally in the army special units or commando units or special fighter units, fighting units tasks. But these were clearly, as what they described to me, police units.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what did they -- what did they tell you as regards to their relationship with the Bosnian Serbs' military forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: They had no real relationship. They said they were from a special unit and they had a special task on the ground in Srebrenica. And I asked how many were there from them, I asked more questions, where they specifically came from and what their task was. I got no any more specific answers because then it became clear to them that I was asking more and more.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what language did you use in speaking to them?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I spoke German. They could speak German perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, I have no more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to make one clarification. On the associated exhibits list, we list a video. But since -- and that is 65 ter 40044 --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Since we will be using the compilation of the Srebrenica trial video, I will not move to admit 40044.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for -- we also already noted the time clip of that -- time for that clip and so that can be removed --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- from the associated exhibits. One question for you, Ms. West. I know that -- and I have to note that your summary does not form the part of evidence, but in one of your summary in -- from line 24, page 30, you referred to a confrontation between the colonel and the lieutenant. I read out: "The colonel also observed what he believed to be a DutchBat lieutenant and some DutchBat soldiers assisting in the deportation of the population by helping the Muslim refugees leave the area. This" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Prosecution mike should be off, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "This resulted in a confrontation between the colonel and the lieutenant, but the process continued." What paragraph do you refer to in this summary, paragraph in the amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm referring to paragraphs 80, 81, and 82.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see a confrontation there?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps that is not clear. May I ask the witness a few questions about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, you've heard the concern of the President. In your amalgamated statement you spoke about interactions with Lieutenant van Duijn. Can you tell us what that's about?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I looked through my camera alongside the line of buses, and it was not a good sight what I saw through the camera lens because it looked like DutchBat was assisting in the deportation. And that was what I spoke with my colleague about. He was not -- he was not at the same opinion as I had. He said there is no problem. We are not assisting. And we got a little bit of confrontation because it's not important, said to him, what you -- what your opinion is, but it gives a -- not a best view on what the UN is doing here on the ground, and that's more important than what your opinion was. So this confrontation ended because another colleague came along and the confrontation stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is this the difference of opinion that you spoke about in paragraph 81?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was a difference of opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And after that confrontation, did the bussing continue?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, it continued. It continued almost immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And both of you are at the same rank, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- no, he was a lieutenant 1st class and I was a lieutenant 2nd class at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please forgive my ignorance, who was higher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1st class, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly requested to speak closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To be clear, all the associated exhibits will be -- had been admitted and given -- will be given a number in due course. Yes, Colonel Rutten, as you see your previous documents, statements, i.e., amalgamated statement, has been admitted in lieu of your examination-in-chief and you will be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. von Rutten. I hope you have heard me. Have you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I heard you perfectly well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you, do you still stand by your positions that you are not willing to make your diaries accessible to us or to disclose them to us?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please call up confidential proofing note if it hasn't been tendered -- if it hasn't been tendered by the Prosecution already, it's 1D04724. Can we have page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see that this is the first time when you refused to make your diaries available; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has this been admitted into evidence? If not, I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a several-page statement in which the witness has now authenticated one statement within this very large document, and I think the entire document has not been authenticated and should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you mean by not having been authenticated? The witness was not asked about this document as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: As I understand it, Mr. Karadzic has asked him about one sentence in this document. He's indicated that that sentence is correct. I suspect if the witness were asked about the document in full, he would not authenticate it, and so I don't think at this point it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, first of all, have we seen the sentence yet? Where do you have it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Still has some photographic material. Is willing to make this available if some indication could be given of what is being looked for. Has photos ..." and so on. "Has a diary containing personal notes which he would rather not make available." [Interpretation] But I'm going to revisit this document at a later stage. However, if this is a problem, let us stick to page 1 for the moment, which is R0138820.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Ms. West, you would not oppose to admitting that one page --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- together with the first page. Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1951, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D04884.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have provided this this month, or at least very recently, and you have confirmed there that you are not prepared to make your diaries available to us; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I have to ask you. If witness confirms the content of this document, is there a point of admitting this document separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, it doesn't need to be admitted. Perhaps it would be better if we clarified the date of this document, which is the 16th of November, 2011, and reflects a conversation on the 14th of November, 2011, but with that addition I think everything in the document has been on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Earlier today in -- on page 34 you said - and that was in response to a question by Judge Kwon, exactly what I would have wanted to ask you - you said: From what I know today and then you stated your opinion. I'm concerned, Mr. von Rutten, how are we going to distinguish between what you knew then and saw then and can confirm as a fact from that time on one hand and what has changed in the meantime and under the influence of the media and other developments on the other?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: First, Mr. Karadzic, my name is Rutten and not von Rutten. I am not of a German noble family, I am a Dutchman. And that is the first thing I want to clarify on that. And next thing is my answer to your question. I answered your question because with the knowledge of today we have far more knowledge on how we perform also in the military in info operations and psychological operations. Then my second sentence was in my clarification to that answer that with -- back then, my opinion was that it stopped immediately after handing out the water and the bread and the candy to the children and what we saw two days later. Because what we saw two days later on -- through satellite communication, on the TV, was a image of perfect -- of a perfect situation of treating the Muslim population in the enclave. And that was not the real situation on the ground in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not interested in that point now. We'll come to that because you've spoken about that more than once. Do you understand why the Defence needs your diary? Because the diary is contemporaneous, whereas your current views and opinions are amalgamated with everything that you've read and seen since. Do you agree that your diary would be of great assistance to us because it reflects what you saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not a perfect person in my remembrance, but since 1995 there have been so many statements on my name in the different documents laid down, so this is the situation that it was. It is not a specific, personal diary; it's just a small book with my notes what happened every day, and that's the small book that I read out before I go to a next -- to make my next -- testify in the next case, nothing more and nothing less. And there are some personal notes to it and that's the reason that I wanted to keep it personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, maybe I could intervene and ask if the witness could be asked whether or not if he would be allowed to redact those personal notes that don't pertain to observations what was happening in Srebrenica, whether he would be willing to give us access to the remainder of the diary other than those that -- items that are personal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Why don't you put your -- put the question yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay, so Colonel Rutten, I'm Peter Robinson, I'm the legal advisor for Dr. Karadzic and I think you heard my question. What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I would not make it available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Why not? Because what I stated earlier. This is a personal document and I want to keep it personal. And the reason for that is, as I stated earlier, that there have been so many documents on my name shortly after the collapse of the enclave that these are specific enough and were in -- put in the time-frame where my memory was fresh enough to clarify all specific events. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And when was the last time you looked at that diary before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I looked in the diary last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. In preparation to refresh your memory for your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I would like to be heard on a motion to compel the witness to produce the diary, but perhaps we can do that outside of his presence or at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rutten, sorry for bestowing upon you this noble title. It was not intentional, but there are many Dutch people who do have a "van" in front of their surname. Have you been promoted in the army since then?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From 2nd lieutenant you have become lieutenant-colonel; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: You're correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what became of your other colleagues, Colonel Karremans and the others, have they remained in the army? Have they been promoted?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
