utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be heard? I don't understand the relevance of any promotion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Agreed. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is relevant because there have been differences of opinion in fates and in careers between Mr. Rutten and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please continue. Move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was your main role in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: My main role was commander of an anti-tank platoon, and since my personnel was working on the observation post my role and task was patrol co-ordinator in the northern part of the enclave and intelligence officer from the company to the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly what is written in paragraph 4 of your statement. That was your second duty. Your first duty was as commander of the anti-tank platoon; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But as an intelligence officer you should have knowledge about the situation and the forces in your surroundings that you were reporting to your superior; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: If we had any sight on them, more than the lines of sight that we had in the enclave, since the enclave is in a much deeper part than the mountains -- up the mountains there where the Serbs were, the VRS were, we should have known more about the specific situation where we had been left in, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've spoken in the Krstic case and in the Tolimir case. I'll tell you the reference now. In Tolimir case on the 12th of September, this year, page 17835; in the Krstic case, 5 April 2000, page 2173; and in the Krstic case again on the same page, you spoke about the inspection of convoys, saying that you have never seen any weapons detected. Did you believe that the inspections should stop because no weapons had been found?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there were never weapons found on those convoys. It's not to my jurisdiction at the moment that -- to stop the VRS from checking the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you are stating that as your objection, grudge, against the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The situation was on the convoys, they came in very less convoys in that period of time. The convoys were checked as they came in through OP Papa in the enclave by the VRS and were checked by us at the moment they were unloaded near the warehouse in Srebrenica city itself. We never saw any weapons came out of these UN convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking rather about your attitude to those inspections. Do you know that according to the Geneva Conventions, the Army of Republika Srpska had the right to inspect not only the transports but also the way the aid was distributed? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As an intelligence officer you've stated your opinion that some military equipment had arrived but not in major quantities. You say that in Krstic, on page 2174, so you were aware that some military equipment was coming in but not in large quantities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We saw some materiel equipment later on during my tour in Srebrenica, that was in the spring-time, but we never could check where it came from exactly. At least, we never saw it come along through one of the UN convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the new uniforms and new Kalashnikovs?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There seemed to be a line through the mountains, through the southern part of the enclave, by the Muslim army, but that happened during the night and we were not in the situation to fully control the southern part of the border of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've also said that you were only half successful in disarming the people within the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica. Do you agree that it was one of your missions to disarm the protected area and make sure that there are no troops and no weapons inside?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. If I can just have a page cite for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if the witness confirms, I don't see why I should waste time on that. It was in the Krstic trial, 2166 is the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was your understanding that they had a small amount of weapons, hand-held launchers, and some mortars. And then at a later point you said that you were only half successful in disarming them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This will always be a problem of disarming the people of the former Republic of Yugoslavia because there are still weapons in former Yugoslavia and we never will manage to disarm this -- these people. Also, we were at that point never in a situation to totally control the disarmament of the Muslim population in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that according to the international laws of warfare and the regulations governing protected areas, somebody must be in charge of disarming protected areas, making sure that there are only civilians inside?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Having weapons does not mean that there are military personnel inside of the enclave. We know the history of former Yugoslavia all very well and I read a lot about it, that the people of former Yugoslavia were always well armed in all these decades before it came through the war in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. We will be offering documents about that. But my question was: Once when an agreement is made on a protected area, it implies that there are only civilians inside being protected, that there are no military and no weapons that can be used?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was supposed to disarm them, the Army of Republika Srpska or the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But UNPROFOR hasn't done it; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We were working on that in the period that we were in the enclave, and we never stated nor my commander stated that we were -- fully completed this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a moment ago that the presence of weapons is not the same as the presence of an army. Do you believe that the 28th Division with thousands of troops was not present in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There were parts of the 28th Division under the command of Naser Oric present in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many of them were there, in your view, or rather, to the best of your knowledge, because you are an intelligence officer you should know that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't have any specific figure on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. You said at some point that these were refugees, that they were not army units; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Most of the people were refugees, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I were to tell you that there were seven formations there within the 28th Division and that they had a communications system and that they communicated every day with the Main Staff and received weapons and assignments, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That could be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I say to you that immediately after the demilitarisation there were 12.000 soldiers left and that to July 1995 the figure went down to 6.000 soldiers, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: If that's the figures that you have present, that could be the situation. We had no specific figures on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D4880 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you exchange your information with your colleagues? Were there any briefings at your staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, there were briefings during the staff meetings. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, for example, what Mr. Franken would know is something that you should be aware of as well; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I was -- that should be, but I was not always present during those briefings because I was patrol co-ordinator as well and I was regularly on foot in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Fair enough, as we say. But then I have to establish what it is that you can testify about in a sovereign manner as opposed to some kind of collateral information. Tell me, have you heard of Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, it's not known specifically to me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put this to you. Sefer Halilovic was the first commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- well, not the supreme commander because that was Mr. Izetbegovic. He was the Chief of Staff. And please take a look at this. In line 5 this is what he writes in numerical terms. He says its numerical size was reduced from 12.000 to about 6.000 soldiers. And further on, he objects on account of that. He's complaining why they reduced the numbers so sharply. But please take a look at this other paragraph. [In English] "Since 1993 ..." [Interpretation] Did you know that the Muslim government was not really interested in Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, it was not to my knowledge at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you surprised then if you read that they kept trying to have this exchanged for the Serb suburbs of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This document -- I see this document for the first time. Now you ask me for a statement. I have to read the full document to give a real explanation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Take a look at the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a large offensive of the Muslim forces against the Serbs that was launched on the 15th of June? [In English] "The operation of deblocking," [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, [In English] "Sarajevo began on the 15th June, 1995, and the Chetniks entered Srebrenica on July 11th ..." [Interpretation] Did you know that there was this large-scale offensive in Sarajevo and that the 28th Division had reinforced its attacks in order to spread out the Serb forces? From the 15th of June onwards they kept attacking the Serb forces. There was a large-scale offensive going on.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: If that's the thing is that herein document, must be, but it is not in my knowledge back then and not now anymore, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that worries me. If you were an intelligence officer and if you were co-ordinator there, a co-ordinator of the observers, how was it that you did not notice that the 28th Division was fully operating against the Serb forces from mid-June until the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I must say, this was not happening in the lines of sight of the enclave. What you are referring to is not directly in the enclave or at the borders of the enclave. There we have not seen this -- these kind of activities against the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But could you tell us first what this document is about? It's allegedly says Mr. Halilovic's book, but in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this had already been admitted somewhere. It has some designation. It has an ERN number, so that is one chapter or one topic from Sefer Halilovic's book "A Cunning Strategy." That was the title of the book. And he touched upon what happened in Srebrenica, inter alia, and he was the supreme commander, or rather, the military Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not asking who Mr. Halilovic was. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In the first instance, the witness has said he's never seen this before. He, in fact, said he didn't know who Halilovic was. One of his answers on page 54, line 15, "If that's the thing herein the document, that must be, but it was not in my knowledge back then and not now anymore." He has in no way authenticated anything at all in this document and should not be admitted through him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It relates to the existence of the 28th Division and as well its number and witness dealt with it. Does it relate to his credibility at all? You do not challenge the authenticity of this document, do you?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I honestly can't say anything about that because this witness has offered us no information as to the authenticity of this document. I'm -- in fact, in regard to the size, he was asked earlier about another part of that document early on, 12 to -- 12.000 to 6.000 soldiers and he said again that it was not within his knowledge at that point. So he can't say anything about the authenticity and nor can the Prosecution at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything to this in -- with respect to the authenticity of this document? Where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously the OTP got a hold of this and put it in the ERN system and it has to do with paragraph 9 of the amalgamated statement, military forces in and around the enclave, and that is what the witness has dealt with. And he says that there was no real military structure -- rather, he said that there was some groups, several hundred men --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm asking about the authenticity, not the content of this document. You said -- I take it that from your words you have no idea what this document is about or where it came from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] EDS, Excellency. It has its number. But I know the book too. It's a well-known book, and I will be using that book frequently. However, this was found in EDS or maybe it was even disclosed to me by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you have no information that you can offer as to this document, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think the Prosecution can be asked to provide information on this document because it's in their collection. The R number tends to indicate that they received it from a Rule 70 provider and that -- we don't have the ability to track -- backtrack through their evidence collection as to where they got it but they can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm just wondering why the need for this discussion and this additional burden on the Prosecution to check the provenance of a document which purports to be an excerpt from a book which the Defence says it has and which it could have used in the first place in this effort and then we would be back to the original question of whether or not the information provided by the witness is sufficient to either properly contextualise or to authenticate the assertions made in the book or whether or not it provides impeachment of the witness's testimony. But why we're focusing on this document instead of the book itself is a little bit of a mystery to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say a word or two?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness about the strength of the Muslim army and the enclave. Paragraph 9 of the amalgamated statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- subparagraph (c) --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the issue I'm dealing with at this moment is only authenticity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we mark it for identification then and we'll show the book; however, we received this from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This document deals with events, according to the accused, which the witness should have known or events that took place while the witness was there. So in that regard, we can -- we have a basis to admit it, but pending the -- we are satisfied as to its authenticity, we will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1952, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we briefly take a look at 1D4885.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this, Mr. Rutten, the 8th Operations Group Srebrenica and on the 17th of August, 1994, that is to say a year and a half after it was declared a safe haven. Look at what the structure was. Then the 280th, the 281th, the 282nd, the 283rd, the 284rd Brigade and an independent battalion in Srebrenica and the 285th Brigade is in Zepa, but that is beyond your area. Look at these units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, seven of them, and in your paragraph 9 you said that there wasn't any real structure there; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There wasn't any structure there at the moment we were there. I never saw this document before. I said we had a very poor information position in the enclave and also through the UN we got very less information on intelligence matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you said that you never knew where their headquarters were and that you never visited their headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that the case because you did not want to do that or because they had placed some restrictions upon you in that respect?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We weren't aware where their headquarters was. This document, what you just showed to me, doesn't indicate that their -- that their headquarters was known by us, meaning DutchBat. What you are showing me here is that there were units in the enclave. But this document is new to me; I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at 65 ter -- sorry, actually, can this be admitted, this telegram?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the origin of this telegram?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My Defence got this from the collection of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the telegram is Naser Oric's response to his Main Staff. The 20th of August, 1994, is the number and there is a number here and everything else. It also has an ERN number in the OTP collection, but I haven't found that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any ERN number and it looks rather new.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a telegram that we got from what my Defence had obtained, but I'm sure that the OTP has this too. You can have it MFI'd and we are going to tell you once we found the Prosecution number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are looking as well. If we could just hold off on this and we can get some more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D1953, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we'll proceed. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now take a look at 65 ter 03231. Let's look at paragraph 2.34. It reads: [In English] "The BiH forces in the enclave were organised into four brigades with a combined strength of 3- to 4.000 men. Their weapons consisted almost exclusively of light arms, supplemented by, among others, a limited number of heavy machine-guns, anti-tank weapons, and mortars. Despite the fact that DutchBat, in accordance with its mission, did everything to disarm the BiH, the battalion was only partly successful. The regular BiH units were reinforced by local militia. Operations were relatively unpredictable, because the units were barely trained and rather undisciplined ...," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this was said at one of the debriefing session at a Dutch ministry or wherever? Are you familiar with this information?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I could have read it through the last 16 years, it could be possible, but there is some information and it supports my remark that there were separate groups because the last sentence says what I stated earlier, and that was what we saw on the ground, barely trained and rather undisciplined units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, since the Prosecution as well tendered just one paragraph of this Dutch debriefing, could you tell us what that Dutch debriefing is about? Whose debriefing it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I can. It actually -- we have tendered I think three paragraphs of this debriefing, and this is the Assen debriefing that was conducted by the Dutch government in September of 1995, where a number of people were interviewed in support of that debriefing and it's over a hundred pages long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the future, why don't you include the first page so that the Chamber can know what that document is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 9 of your statement is somewhat flawed. There was a structure in existence, but in that paragraph you said that you didn't have information to the effect that the BH army was leaving the enclave and carrying out operations outside of it. From here we can see that they had taken actions that were unpredictable because they were not disciplined; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to see para 9 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we upload it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have an extra copy. Would that be easier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would be more convenient. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may draw your attention to the fact that you heard of it from Major Nikolic, and from other paragraphs in your statement one can see that you didn't believe a thing that the Serbs said and you didn't check this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That isn't correct completely because we were not simply in the position to check this because we could not wander over the border of the enclave because that was all -- we had no freedom of movement outside of the enclave, so we -- weren't even possible to check it for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you send a report about what Major Nikolic told you, which was that the previous night they went out of the enclave, killed some people, and set some villages on fire? Did you report this to anyone?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: What you're now doing is that you are putting a statement to a certain date or moment, but that was not the case. Constantly the VRS was speaking to us about situations that might have happened, but since we were not in control or had no freedom of movement to check it, it had no sense of checking all these rumours from all kinds of people to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you disputing that these forces that you were supposed to disarm and that you were supposed to turn this area into a demilitarised zone had set fire on numerous Serb villages and killed around 4.000 people, mostly civilians, and that only a few of them were soldiers? Are you disputing or denying that you knew this?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that. I'm not denying that. We were at that point not aware what happened out of our lines of sight. As I stated earlier in my earlier answers, we could only see, and that is also in paragraph 9 of the document that it was handed to me, what I said right there: "Even standing at the border of the enclave, for example, at OP Oscar in November, it was not possible to see Serb villages in our line of sight, thus we would have not been in the position to see any attacks on these villages." So it's in the document that it's provided. I don't see the relevance of this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But are you aware that those were the units that were under your protection? How was it possible that you didn't see them going out, plundering, and being involved in various activities?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Our battalion had only three and a half hundred soldiers -- I mean infantry personnel. That means that a lot of them was not in the enclave itself because the VRS had not let them go back, after leave, go into the enclave again. So we had a very difficult situation inside of the enclave to even man the OPs at that point with a very few personnel left - I mean and then personnel left, not logistic personnel but infantry personnel left in the enclave. So we weren't simply -- it wasn't simply possible to have a clear look on the borders itself. So I don't see -- also again you know -- you knew the situation of the DutchBat. I don't see again no relevance of this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Akashi know about this? If you didn't know, how come that Mr. Akashi knew about it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D4882, please. 1D4882.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from January 1994, a telegram sent by Mr. Akashi to the Secretary-General and for information of Kofi Annan.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 4 where Mr. Akashi explains that rotations are not the problem that the Serbs see as such, but rather control and proper usage of the airfields and the safe haven. And if you look at the paragraph at the bottom, it says that the Bosnian government has taken tactical advantage of the presence of UNPROFOR beyond the stated objectives of the relevant Security Council Resolutions. And the last two lines on this page: [In English] "While this objective has been achieved by UNPROFOR's presence, the Bosnian Muslim forces have recently embarked on an increasingly offensive approach, partly using the safe areas as a staging ground. For the Bosnian Serbs this is a cause of great concern which has led them to question UNPROFOR's impartiality increasingly. In the political preparations for the two operations, therefore, it has to be kept in mind that the situation has changed as regards Security Council Resolutions 836 and 844." [Interpretation] So, Mr. Rutten, can you see that His Excellency, Mr. Akashi, had information that this area was being abused as a spring-board or as a basis for mounting attacks on the Serbian positions, whereas you knew nothing about that? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: You better ask Mr. Akashi, because he is in command. I'm not in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There are other crucial elements here; however, I don't have sufficient time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't doubt the authenticity of this, but this witness can't affirm anything in this document. I would also point out that this document is dated January 26, 1994, and this witness has only gotten to Srebrenica a couple weeks before. So this is just not the appropriate vehicle for this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. I misspoke. This is a 1994 document, not 1995. So the witness wasn't there until over a year later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The issue concerning the abuse of safe haven was even worse in 1995 than in 1994. That was an ongoing practice. Therefore, this reflects the situation that persisted with regard to the abuse of safe areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, having heard that Colonel Rutten arrived in Srebrenica only in 1995, we can't say this relates to his credibility. We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, we'll take a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I kindly ask you to reconsider the issue of time allocated to me. I would like to have more time because there are quite a few paragraphs here that can be challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have to focus on important issues. Still you have more than an hour. I think that may be sufficient for you. We'll take a break for 25 minutes and resume at ten to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rutten, I must show you quickly a number of documents that might refresh your memory with regard to the events that took place whilst you were there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D04699.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Muslim forces in Srebrenica were very hostile towards you, they used to stop you, to restrict your movement, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We never had directly problems with the Muslims in the enclave, so what you're stating is, to me, not correct in the period I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please have the English translation of 4699 or can it be shown in some other way? Perhaps to put it on ELMO. This document is dated the 28th of January, 1995, when you were there and it says that your movement is restricted in the general area of Suceska and Podgaj. It also says here that the commander of the DutchBat in Srebrenica order his patrols to enter the area which was off limits for movement. Therefore, is it true that there were areas to which you were denied access?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is known to me because this was a period in January where there were some problems with the BiH commander in that area. And finally it resolved sometime later in January 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But did you have access to the Bandera triangle?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That was the triangle near OP Alpha. That was -- that we had some restriction in movement for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that you had free access everywhere around the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, we had free access, except this -- what happened in early January 1995 because it was shortly after we were -- we were in command of the enclave because the former battalion had left, and shortly afterwards they more or less tested us whether -- how we would react if they would restrict our freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is the original? Do you have any idea, Ms. West, as to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The B/C/S version is a translation of English version or the vice versa?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that this is in the system and the B/C/S is the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The B/C/S what -- that we are seeing now?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the whole page because there's a number at the top. This is the original. It's a telegram sent by the 8th Operations Group, and we have a translation on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1956, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have now 1D04701 and we have the translation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that the Serbian side had asked for Zepa to be declared not a demilitarised zone because we were exposed to attacks coming from it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is all about Zepa area, and I'm not familiar with this kind of information, nor was I at that point, in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But look at this order which pertains to the 8th Operations Group, not only to Zepa, and under 2 or in paragraph 2 it says that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot find the particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then there's a mention of helicopters, that they have to be disguised, and in talks with UNPROFOR a position should be taken, maintaining that the helicopters were used for the transportation of political representatives of Srebrenica and Zepa, et cetera. Don't you see that they have made a plan to conceal their activities in the safe areas and that they successfully have hidden their military involvement?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is about the Zepa area. I'm not familiar with the things that happened in the Srebrenica itself because it isn't mentioned in this document specifically. They are speaking here about the Ukrainian Battalion that was stationed in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Rutten, if you look at items 1, 2, and 3, it refers to the entire 8th Operations Group and there is mention of Srebrenica. It also says these units are going to be placed in combat-readiness in order to act in co-ordination with Zepa and that that should be kept secret. So this entirely refers to Srebrenica as well. Under number 6 it says: "The command of the 2nd Corps will carry out the preparatory activities given in the Directive, in connection with the engagement of forces in the direction towards the protected areas of Srebrenica and Zepa." Were you aware that right next to you military operations were being carried out and that it particularly involved Srebrenica and Zepa? In addition to that, do you know that for that reason the Serbian army wanted this designation "demilitarised" to be removed? Here we have an admission on the part of the BH army and a statement that they were carrying out these activities as clandestine activities.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We had no possibility to see these documents, at least not to my knowledge. And I think that they have succeeded in -- to keep it of -- to do this operation secretly because we weren't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rutten. I don't expect you to know the document. I expect you to know about the event that it describes, but anyway I'm happy with the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that. Mr. -- Colonel Rutten, did you say that you were not there at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was not there and -- because I see this document for the first time. We were not aware that these - that's these activities - were happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. This document is dated as 17th of February, 1995, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- sorry, sir, I was there, but I said also they succeeded in -- to do this operation secretly because we as DutchBat weren't aware of these activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1955, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 1D4704. I think there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this, Mr. Rutten. This is from 8 July, the command of the 28th Division, or rather, the command of the 2nd Corps writes about the combat performance of the units and commands of the 28th Division. And although encircled, it says they decided to contribute to the maximum to the fight against the aggressor so they increased their activities deep in the temporarily occupied territory. Their purpose is to prevent enemy forces from sending additional troops to the Sarajevo theatre of operations from the area around Srebrenica and Zepa by causing losses, primarily human losses, which would force the aggressor to tie-up troops in the wider area of Srebrenica and Zepa. And then it says that their successful sabotage actions behind enemy lines achieved the following: 60 Chetniks were liquidated and a lot of materiel was seized, 16 automatic rifles, three light machine-guns, et cetera: "In the village of Visnjica, large quantities of ammunition was seized, but the soldiers were so exhausted that they could not remove it, so the ammunition was destroyed, as were all the facilities that the aggressor could possibly use for military purposes." Do you believe that such a weak and disorganised army can make excursions behind the lines of the Serb army, burn down villages, seize dozens of enemy soldiers, seize materiel, et cetera? Were you aware of these operations? Is this this weak force you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This document is new to me because it's -- it was not in our possession during the period that I was in the enclave, and we were not aware. I tried to explain you earlier that we only had our lines of sight. We were poorly equipped and we had a very poor information situation with UNPROFOR, so we were not aware what was happening next to our lines of sight. You speak of a wider area around the enclave of Srebrenica and Zepa. Our battalion had no information whatsoever on these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rutten, these are forces that went out of the protected area, killed people, burned down all the buildings that the army could possibly use, and when it says "buildings" it means houses; and they were doing that in co-ordinated action with the 1st Corps in Sarajevo -- it doesn't say explicitly the 1st Corps, but we know what it means, so that Serbs could not send their soldiers to the area of Sarajevo. And the last lines say: Use this information only for internal information to the commands and units of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that means it was to be kept from you and it was kept from you. I'm trying to say, Mr. Rutten, that your positions and your statements are not based on facts. I'm not criticising you or blaming you, but the fact is that this did happen on the 8th of July, as recorded by this document of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those are the forces, Muslim forces, that went out of the protected area and launched attacks; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. What we see are several lines of the accused just making a statement. And the only question at the end is: Is my statement correct? I don't see this as a legitimate question to the witness and it should be excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I disagree. You can ask -- you can put an assertion and ask a witness: Isn't that correct? We're taught to do that in cross-examination. That's what even Judge Morrison, I think, has been suggesting to Dr. Karadzic to make his question more pointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, could you expand on --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. This is not only just an assertion, but this is more in lines of a closing argument and the defendant is just looking for the witness -- to make his closing argument and whether the witness says "yes" or "no," I would submit, is not his reason for the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, there are some points which are rather argumentative in your question, Mr. Karadzic. While I see the point of putting your case, I think you could have been a bit simpler. But can I ask whether you can answer the question, though?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This -- the problem is that if any army or group of people who want to do secretly actions and they do it during the night in a very big area, in fact, where only less than 400 UN personnel, infantry personnel I mean, are available to guard this total enclave in a mountainous area, it's simply not possible to guard such an area and that was also stated at the moment we came into the enclave, that we had too less troops to not only safe-guard the Muslim people, but also to have a good situation on the ground itself. So this is -- this is giving someone a job that he -- with no equipment and no personnel enough to do this job properly. This -- that is what you see right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not disputing that. I'm just going to make it simpler, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- you heard the witness's answer to the effect that he did not know the whole situation. This -- I don't see any point of your keeping asking similar questions. Your time is limited. I think it's time to come to the real issues about the refugees, separation of male, and the nine bodies, et cetera. There are many important issues you can focus.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will move to that immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me just simplify my question. Mr. Rutten, if you had seen that action and if you had known what they were doing, would your conclusion about their force and capabilities have remained the same as recorded in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, it would not have been the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I have enough time at the end I'll come back to this subject, but now I have to move as quickly as possible to this event, the month of July. You described your meetings with the civilian leadership of Srebrenica. Did you also meet with the military leadership and were you quite clear about who was the chief there, who was the commander, who the deputies were?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We had an overall picture of -- at least we had on the northern part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean I should ask you only about the northern part of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes, because my company was -- that was the area of responsibility of the Charlie Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What's the name of that locality where you were? Is it Suceska? What is the name of the broader area?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't know what you exactly mean right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which Muslim brigade covered that area where you worked as its own area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I'm not exactly -- it's not exactly in my recollection right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you meet with the commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. Only the second in command, Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to move quickly now but you know your statement well, don't you. At that time you saw some Dutchmen helping the evacuation of refugees and then you assaulted Serb soldiers, you said it was inappropriate, et cetera, and that was in the presence of Mr. van Duijn.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I never assaulted Serb soldiers. I don't see where you read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you perhaps didn't assault them, but you protested with them, you said it was inappropriate, you expressed your disagreement.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic, it's not perhaps. I never assaulted a Serb soldier, so let's be clear about that. I protested not to the Serb soldier because that so-called Mr. Mana [phoen], who was near Mr. van Duijn - it was a nickname, Mr. Mana - was not in the conversation with me and Mr. van Duijn. I had a conversation with a fellow lieutenant and he was intervening. That was the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps I was not precise enough. In any case, you had a dispute with Mr. van Duijn about whether it was a good idea for the Dutch Battalion to be involved in that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know why Mr. van Duijn had a different opinion? Or to put it differently, do you know what the United Nations demanded from us as far as the refugees are concerned?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Not at that point. Later on I saw some documents -- I saw a very new document to me in the case Tolimir, but at that point I wasn't aware of the documents from the United Nations. Mr. van Duijn and I had a different opinion on the role of the UN at that very point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly look at D1039.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did not participate in negotiations at the level of Akashi, Karadzic, Mladic. You came and expressed your opinion without knowing anything that preceded these actions?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No. I was -- Lieutenant van Duijn was involved in the negotiations at the level of Akashi, Karadzic and Mladic. It was the situation what we had on the ground and he was trying to help the refugees to get quickly out of the enclave. And to me it was that the situation that we more or less helped with the transportation, or rather, deportation of the Muslim population out of the enclave. And that was what we knew at the ground at that point. We were not aware of the document that has been shown here on the computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case your qualification of that evacuation would not be accurate, absent this information? In other words, if you had known what Mr. Akashi was demanding from us, you would not have called the evacuation what you called it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I'm arguing that because Mr. Akashi - and I'm not questioning Mr. Akashi's documents -- but he had no clear view on what was really happening on the ground on the activities of the VRS army. And that was something completely different from what was told in the negotiations to Mr. Akashi. And earlier I stated about the distribution of bread and water and candy to the children, that also gives a different situation than what -- than what --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Please let me conclude my answer. That gives also a completely different situation -- view on the situation on the ground. So that is what was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the passage relating to Dutch troops number 2.(a), where it says Dutch troops will be ordered to do so and so. Did you receive these orders?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I never received these -- those orders, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else receive orders? Was Mr. Akashi the supreme commander, the civilian head of your army, the army of United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not questioning the authority of Mr. Akashi. What I was -- what I'm trying to say is that we were not aware in the early days of July what was happening and what was stated here in the document. That came later on, probably to my commander, but I wasn't aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That means you were not well-positioned to make any comments about the evacuation of the refugees. You should have left it to Mr. Franken and Mr. Karremans, who did have this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just note, there's no evidence that Franken or Karremans had this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We've established that you, Mr. Rutten, were not at the top of the chain of command in order to receive documents like this; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Muslim army asked the United Nations to talk us into evacuating the entire population of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was never mentioned at your briefings, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the second paragraph: [In English] "Following consultations with the Bosnian government, and in order to avoid a continuing humanitarian catastrophe, agreement will be solicited from the Bosnian Serbs to allow all residents of Srebrenica, including all men, to leave for Tuzla if they so wish." [Interpretation] You did not know about this, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, I was not aware about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the next. [In English] "The Dutch will be instructed to remain in the Srebrenica enclave at least until arrangements have been negotiated and finalised with Bosnian Serb authorities for the departure from the enclave of those people." [Interpretation] You did not know that those were your orders; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you attend two meetings, there was one meeting on the 11th and another on the 12th, between Mladic and your representatives as well as the representatives of the Muslims at the Fontana Hotel? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you hear that on the 12th Mladic stated that he had no buses and he asked the United Nations to provide them?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: At that point in 1995 I was not aware of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You found out later?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yeah, we heard about it. Years later we heard about all these happenings, but not -- not in the sequence that you are telling right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you recall that Mladic had not even prepared the fuel and that he asked for you, the UN, to provide fuel for the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just intervene here. The witness has indicated that he did not attend those first two meetings, but nonetheless Dr. Karadzic asked him a question about the meetings. He said he wasn't aware, and now he's asking further questions. I would like to clarify if these are statements made by Mladic at those two meetings and if they are, this witness is not in a position to answer them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Agreed. Mr. Karadzic, your time is limited. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that these questions are legitimate because they have to do with the unit, the one that this officer belonged to. All right. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rutten, who brought the civilians to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Mostly the civilians were forced to walk up to Potocari, and our battalion tried to help the people who were not able to walk up to Potocari. And the force that came from the VRS army who was pressing from the south part of the enclave up to the northern part and the people tried to save themselves from the hostile fire of the VRS army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So when you say "forced," was it the developments themselves that forced them to act in this way or did someone come and tell them they should go to Potocari? Who was it, if so. And did they arrive in Potocari considerably before the Serbs entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The Serbs had already or at least the VRS army had already entered the enclave in the southern part some days earlier by overrun OP Echo. So, in fact, they were in UN territory. Later on there came heavily fire in the southern part, also to our blocking, to the UN blocking positions, and at a certain point to the city of Srebrenica. At that point, the civilians in the town of Srebrenica had to leave the town. At that point, we gave the order, at least the battalion gave the order, to get as much support to the civilian population and the refugees of Srebrenica to safe hold them near Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Rutten, that the civilian authorities informed the citizens and told them to go to Potocari considerably before the Serb army got close to these villages and significantly before the Serb army entered Srebrenica, the town itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That seems very reasonable that the Muslim authorities did that because of the happenings in the other parts of former Yugoslavia. That was the experience they worked on because the VRS army didn't go very softly on the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you, Mr. Rutten. I'm asking you whether you know that this was ordered by the civilian authorities. Your expansion is not well-intentioned and it is partial at that. So you accept that this could have been done by the civilian authorities, that it was ordered by the civilian authorities who did the right thing by doing that; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: It's not only what I knew at that time, what the civilian authorities ordered, but also at this point. If you saying that I am partial, that is an estimation from your side and I would like to leave it to that. The only thing that I have to say is if you are in a civilian governance of saving your own people by an army who is coming up, then as early as possible you have to safe hold your civilians or your refugees. And that is, in my opinion, what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards your differences with Mr. van Duijn, did you know -- actually, you say here that -- let's just find where you said this. You actually called it something very unpleasant, the word that you used for this evacuation. Did you know what the position of the Muslim leadership was vis-a-vis the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: What's your exact question? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You and your colleague had different views with regard to the evacuation. Did you know whether the Muslim civilian authorities would have agreed with you or with your colleague? Did you know what their position was?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That's not of any interest to me because I have my own responsibility as a member of the UN forces on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this opposition to evacuation, was that part of your duty?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I already gave you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that you saw nine persons killed. Did you see the killing itself?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No, we didn't see the killing itself. Shortly afterwards we came to the site where the people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do you know where they had been killed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We could see at the point where they were lying that they hadn't been moved since they were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you saw it just like that. But do you know that it is necessary to conduct an investigation in order to reach such a conclusion? Did you carry out an on-site investigation with regard to these killings?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: There was no marks of transporting these people. They were shot at that -- at that point and they hadn't been moved. We had no time to carry out an on-site investigation because shortly after I had made some pictures we were shot at by the VRS army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm asking you, Mr. Rutten. In order to present this before a court of law, that people had been killed on that site, that had to be subjected to an on-site investigation. Is that what you did or did you rely on your own impression?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The short period of time that we had on this specific spot, we had to rely on our own impression. And we were with two other colleagues and they had the same impression as I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You took documents and when some Serb soldiers got close to you, you ordered to have these documents thrown away; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: We were, in fact, after the blocking positions, so if we had to go back through the blocking positions and through the lines where the VRS military personnel were around, they could discover then what we have been doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha. Thank you. So you didn't want to have the documents found on you. Now I'm going to ask you about the documents that belonged to the prisoners. I'm saying that it was not in the interest of the Serb army for the documents not to be associated with a particular person. The interest in getting rid of the documents was the interest of those prisoners who could have expected an investigation. Did you find out who it was that got rid of their documents?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: If you referring to the documents that were piled up in front of the white house, I expect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: In earlier case, in the Tolimir case, I explained extensively how we work in the military when we want to discover whether civilians are military personnel or not. We do that according to the Geneva Convention, and we save all documents belonging to the people that we detain. In this specific case in front of the white house all civilians were forced to leave their belongings and to get rid of their documents, and that documents are passports, working permits, and so on. So there was no reason for that to get rid of these documents. The only reason I can imagine is that you don't want any identification of the personnel you are detaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Rutten, were we not interested in having them identified, whereas they were not interested in being identified. So it's actually the other way around. The investigation organs want to have them identified and the possible perpetrator is trying to get rid of his documents so that he could not be identified. Did you see who it was that was throwing documents away?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: VRS military was standing in front of the white house, forcing with weapons, pointing with weapons, that they had to get rid of their ID, I mean Muslim civilians, also youngsters, boys from aged 12 years old. And then they were held in the house and later on transported. So I don't think that this is the other way around. VRS was clearly undertaking an operation that is not accordingly to the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see them taking their documents from them and throwing them away? Did you see that with your very own eyes?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I saw with my very own eyes that VRS military pointed at person -- at civilians with their weapons that they had to get rid of their personal belongings and their IDs. That is what I saw, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, your description was that by the time you arrived there the IDs were already on a pile; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I was on several occasions outside and inside the white house. These pile of IDs and belongings grow -- was growing every time I was around, and the next day the whole pile was burning. So there was no reason to take these IDs from these civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 65 ter 19458.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Rutten, that the Serb military intelligence had a list of almost 400 persons -- actually, 387 war criminals who had committed specific crimes against Serb civilians. They were members of the 28th Division. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I was not aware of this list in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the list and look at the last page, and you will see that this was compiled on the 12th of July, 1995, and here you can see that the assumption is that they are still in Srebrenica. Do you agree that many had left through the forest. You, yourself, saw them parting with their families; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: One night earlier I was aware of the fact that large quantities of Muslim men, some with family, left the enclave. It is under the assumption then that these people were still around the Muslim population who was still in the enclave and was transported or deported by the VRS army then. It was not to my knowledge then that these people were under the population that was left in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So far, Mr. Rutten, you've never said that Serbs used weapons to take IDs away from Muslim prisoners. You never said that, not a single time. This is the first time you're saying it. So you saw this thrown onto a pile and you think that you saw this being set on fire, but so far you have not said that the IDs were taken away by having weapons used; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: The VRS military was carrying weapons in front of their chests, so they don't have to point whether they were saying that to the civilians and they did not did that at gunpoint. That wasn't necessary because all these -- the total population was in total fear. And then there is something you are saying that this is the first time that I said that it was being set on fire. I even gave to this Court a picture that I made myself of the pile burning, and that picture I made from out of the enclave you could see the pile burning in front of the white house. So I think there is enough said on this point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have this image displayed. I think that we know what the number is. 65 ter 2733.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, let me ask you, Mr. Rutten, is it correct that Muslim detainees were not only getting rid of their documents but also their money and everything else so that the Serbs would not find them?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just intervene here that the way this is said: "Is it correct that Muslim detainees were not only getting rid of their documents but also their money ..." That would suggest that these detainees are themselves jettisoning their IDs on their own volition, and that's not been the evidence. The evidence is that they were forced to give up their IDs as they were coming up to the house because the Serbian soldiers were making them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was he referring to the evidence in formulating his question, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can be corrected on that if that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us proceed. Can you answer the question, Colonel Rutten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing I witnessed in getting rid of the money was that one moment I was around with the sergeant-major. Some VRS personnel were standing under the staircase asking for money and they stopped giving money the moment we arrived. That was the only time that I saw something happening with money.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Muslims themselves were trying to get rid of their money so that it would not fall into Serb hands?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: That is a statement from your side. I'm not aware of that, as I stated earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, take a look at what you said in your statement. [In English] Royal Netherlands Srebrenica debriefing. [Interpretation] This interview was conducted on the 6th of September, 1995. ERN number is 013889 up until 883 on page 11. You said that they had informed you from the 108th - I don't know what this 108th is - that the Muslims had offered them money but that they would not take it because they wanted -- or actually did not want that money to fall into Serb hands. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: One on the date were two soldiers from the commando company, commando platoon, in fact, that were around the house, they informed me about that, that's right. But they hadn't accept the money from the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's what you state and that they didn't take it. They wouldn't accept it, but the Muslims did want to get rid of the money; whereas you believed that they did not want to get rid of the documents that could identify them and expose them to danger if they are on the list; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Now you are connecting getting rid of the money not by force together with get rid of your documents by force, and force does not always mean force by hand but just being around as the VRS and then in control of the total area and in control of the deportation. The people were in total fear this, so they weren't -- they themselves don't want to get rid of them -- of the documents they were giving the order to get rid of the documents. That's something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have that picture returned, 2733, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rutten, they didn't want the Serbs to take Srebrenica either, but that happened nevertheless. Did you see that anyone was frightened in those images that were displayed during your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't understand your question. Is it what you mean what happened in the white house or what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What we saw. The people who are receiving bread and who are discussing things with Serb soldiers, did you see any fear there or was this just normal behaviour?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: These people hadn't been fed for days, so they were gladly accepting anything. Where I saw total fear along the bus line, where people were forced into buses, I saw total fear in the white house, where I took pictures of all the men and very young men, even youngsters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the photograph, and you claim that it's documents that are on fire here; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: Yes. I had to take this picture from some distance because near the gate itself it wasn't very appropriate to take that picture, but I saw that the pile that was burning over there was the pile of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there a date anywhere, a date for this photograph, and did you see who it was that set this pile on fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: This happened in the day after the 13th, after the -- most of the Serbs had left already. And this pile was already burning during the night, and during the day I made this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see who had set it on fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since today was the first time that you expanded your accusations levelled against the Serbs - I hope that the Trial Chamber will give me more time tomorrow - is it possible that as time goes by you keep making stronger accusations against the Serbs? What is this affected by, the media furor and everything that is happening in courts?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: In all my earlier statements are the words that I already used. If you see all my statements since 1995 you see a strong line of what I earlier stated. These lines are consistent and are being given to different hearings in the Netherlands and abroad. So this is the only answer I can give to you on your estimation on what I'm just right saying on the VRS military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see the Serbs commit any war crime?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I don't know what you specifically aim at at this point, because you are quitely broadly and generally speaking about war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you at that time see with your very own eyes the Serbs committing any war crime?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES RUTTEN
utterances.text: I was around in the white house where I saw a man - and I'll just give you one simple example - who was hanging on the staircase at one arm. I asked the VRS soldier to lower that man. It was a civilian to my eyes, at least he was in civilian clothes, and there was no real reason to keep him there. I saw also very young people in custody in the white house. These were boys from 12 till 15 years old, all in civilian clothes. So I don't see why an army is keeping civilian personnel into custody and transport them with buses out of the enclave to an uncertain destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that right now in Sarajevo there is a protest taking place by the persons who were minors then and were soldiers, nevertheless, and had not received compensations? Do you know that it is precisely today and yesterday that the former 14- and 15-year-olds are protesting in Sarajevo and they were fighters at the time, 15 and 14 years old?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Mr. Karadzic, your time is up. And the Chamber is not minded to give you extra time. Further, separate from the fact, I was advised just now that the witness would not be available tomorrow. Is that information correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I might put a last question now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would allow you to continue till ten past with the indulgence of the staff. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to leave it to Ms. West, but I was a little quicker on my feet. I think she may -- would be requesting at least a modicum of time for re-direct. I suppose no more than -- well, I'll let her speak on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would need only five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
